text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's German newspapers:
- Bonn will drop its opposition to the employment chapter due to be discussed at the Amsterdam summit on EU treaty reforms but will not hand over substantial new powers in the area to Brussels.

- Government coalition leaders meet on Wednesday in a further attempt to agree ways of balancing the budget. Further cuts in the Federal Labour Office funds are "quite unlikely", a senior government figure is quoted as saying.

- Despite the uncertainty surrounding the tax reform, a parliamentary committee is close to concluding its consultations over the corresponding 1999 tax reform law, with discussions due next week on clauses relating to the taxation of pensions and life insurance funds.

- Paris may after all be ready to agree to the stability pact for Europe's monetary union at the Amsterdam summit next week. The German government meanwhile says it is ready to withdraw its long-standing resistance to an employment chapter in the new Maastricht Treaty
- The new head of the main German construction employers federation says non-German companies should pay wages at the same level as their domestic rivals in the German market.
- Further crisis meetings are due Wednesday and Thursday between government coalition politicians to iron out differences on how to stop up budget gaps.
- Mannesmann defends its leading position in the German telecom market, reaching some 2.7 million customers in the first half of the year.

- Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats are seeking to increase tax receipts by bringing forward part of the planned future tax reform that aims to slash currently available tax breaks. Junior coalition partners the FDP however oppose such a move as "disguised tax increases".
- May German inflation accelerates again, rising to 1.6 percent from 1.4 percent the month before.
- Transport minister Matthias Wissmann issues a call for increased transport infrastructure in Germany, but says such projects must not be driven by the state alone.
